newsitem.title: GERMANY: Ransom recovered, five held in German kidnap case.
newsitem.headline: Ransom recovered, five held in German kidnap case.

text.p: German police have recovered four million marks ($2.6 million) in ransom money paid to the kidnappers of multi-millionaire Jakub Fiszmann and have arrested five people, prosecutors said on Wednesday.
But a spokesman for the prosecutors' office said it was not known whether the Frankfurt businessman, who was kidnapped on October 1, was still alive.
The spokesman said police had arrested three German men and two women in connection with the kidnapping. He said that despite searches there was still no indication as to where Fiszmann was.
"These are the main suspects," said Klaus-Juergen Timm, head of criminal investigations in the state of Hesse.
"We don't know whether or not Mr Fiszmann is alive. In the interests of the victim and as long as we have no proof to the contrary we are working on the basis he is alive," he said.
Timm told the news conference in Wiesbaden that police were not ruling out the possibility there were more people involved in the kidnapping.

The suspects, who were aged between 26 and 51 years, had in part confessed to the crime, prosecutor Reiner Schilling told the news conference. One of the women had worked in Fiszmann's property firm for 10 years.
The ransom money was found in the garden of a flat in Wiesbaden, with two 1,000 mark notes ($650) missing.
Authorities said previously they believed Fiszmann was still alive even though the kidnappers had reneged on a promise to free him after the ransom was paid last week.
Earlier on Wednesday police said they had detained two men and a woman and searched buildings and apartments in Frankfurt, Wiesbaden and Mainz.
Fiszmann, a 40-year old businessman and member of one of Germany's richest families, was abducted outside his Frankfurt office just over two weeks ago.
The only contact with Fiszmann since then has been a phone call he made to a contact, believed to be his girlfriend, saying he was being kept in a cellar.
Fiszmann's brother Georg paid the ransom on October 10 for his release, but his kidnappers failed to free him as promised the following day.
Police said on Tuesday they believed Fiszmann was still alive, following a statement from the kidnappers that the victim had enough provisions to survive for four weeks.

Earlier this week, police searched a former U.S. army arms depot in the Frankfurt area. Searchers used helicopters and tracker dogs to comb the area after an anonymous telephone caller said cars believed to have been used for the kidnap had been seen in the area.
Police have also been monitoring the sale of medication which Fiszmann needs to treat acute food allergies.
Fiszmann runs a property and electronics company in Frankfurt and is also known locally for financing the production of the musical "Tommy" in Offenbach near Frankfurt.
Police believe that his abductors may be part of the same gang who unsuccessfully tried to extort money during an aborted kidnap of Fiszmann's nephew in 1991.
It appears Fiszmann tried to fight off his kidnappers as his broken wristwatch and small amounts of blood were found in a white van used in the abduction and later recovered by police.
